The page holds two complete tables of biquadratic (quartic) residue classes. Each table has the same layout as the previous page (p = 157, 173, 181, 193) and the next page (p = 277, 269).

Header data (for each prime p ≡ 1 mod 4):
- g is a primitive root mod p.
- f = g^((p-1)/4) mod p, so f^2 ≡ -1 (mod p).
- p = a^2 + b^2, with a ≡ 1 (mod 4) and b even.
- The sign of b is fixed by the congruence a + b f ≡ 0 (mod p). This is my inference: it holds for every entry on this and the neighbouring pages. Equivalently, f is the image of i in Z[i]/(a+bi). The previous page writes the same data as -11-6i, +13+2i, etc.

Classes: the residues 1..p-1 are split by ind_g(x) mod 4.
- A: index ≡ 0 (biquadratic residues).
- B: index ≡ 1.
- C: index ≡ 2.
- D: index ≡ 3.
Each class has (p-1)/4 members.

(1) p = 293, g = 2, f = 138, a = 17, b = +2.
- 293 = 17^2 + 2^2.
- 138^2 = 19044 = 65·293 - 1, so 138^2 ≡ -1.

  - 2^16 ≡ -96
  - 2^32 ≡ 133

  - 2^73 = 2^64·2^8·2 ≡ 109·(-37)·2 ≡ -155 ≡ 138. ✓
- 2 is a primitive root: 2^146 ≡ -1 and 2^4 ≠ 1.
- 17 + 2·138 = 293 ≡ 0. ✓
- Class A begins 1, 16 (= 2^4), …; B begins 2, …; C begins 4, …; D begins 8, …. Class A has 73 entries.
- Since 293 ≡ 5 (mod 8), -1 has index 146 ≡ 2, so x ↦ -x swaps A↔C and B↔D. Spot checks all hold: 1↔292, 16↔277, 17↔276, 22↔271, 2↔291, 3↔290, 5↔288, 7↔286, 162↔131, 233↔60, 211↔82.
- Quadratic-character checks (A∪C = quadratic residues) hold for 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23.

(2) p = 281, g = 3, f = 228, a = +5, b = +16.
- 281 = 5^2 + 16^2.
- 228^2 = 51984 = 185·281 - 1.
- Check that f = g^70 (my verification):
  - 3^10 ≡ 39
  - 3^20 ≡ 116
  - 3^40 ≡ -32
  - 3^70 ≡ (-32)(116)(39) ≡ -53 ≡ 228. ✓
- 3 is a primitive root: 3^140 ≡ -1, 3^56 ≡ 86, 3^40 ≢ 1.
- 5 + 16·228 = 3653 = 13·281. ✓
- Here 281 ≡ 1 (mod 8), so -1 ∈ A and every class is closed under x ↦ -x. Checks hold: 2↔279, 3↔278, 5↔276, 15↔266, 87↔194, 190↔91. Class D has 70 entries.

Purpose: this is inductive raw material for the theory of biquadratic residues (Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum).
- The table yields the quartic character of small primes as a function of (a, b).
- In particular, across all seven primes on pages 53–55, the class of 2 is index b/2 mod 4:
  - b ≡ 0 (mod 8) → A (281: b = 16)
  - b ≡ 2 (mod 8) → B (293, 157, 173, 181, 269)
  - b ≡ 4 (mod 8) → C (193)
  - b ≡ 6 (mod 8) → D (277)
- This is exactly Gauss's published theorem on the biquadratic character of 2 (Comm. prima, 1828), which he said he found by induction.
- 2 ∈ A for 281 also matches 281 = 5^2 + 64·2^2.
- The ±3 summary table on the previous page shows the same use for 3.

The page contains no derivations, only computed lists.

results.what: Empirical data consistent with: 2 lies in class (b/2) mod 4 when a + b f ≡ 0
results.modern_name: biquadratic character of 2 (quartic residuosity of 2; supplementary law of quartic reciprocity)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss 1828 (found by induction from such tables); 2 quartic residue iff p = x^2 + 64y^2 (Gauss, Dirichlet)

deep.surprise_reason: These are computational tables of biquadratic residues of exactly the kind Gauss described using for his 1828 induction on the quartic character of 2 (and later of other primes). They match his published theorems and contain nothing beyond what is known to be his.
